item: Jayatunga et al. 2024 Phase I denominator (n of molecules on which the 80-90% rate is computed)
queries_tried: (1) 'Jayatunga Drug Discovery Today AI-discovered molecules Phase I success rate 80-90% clinical'; (2) 'Jayatunga 2024 Drug Discovery Today AI-discovered molecules Phase I n=24 Phase II n=10 sample size companies'; (3) 'Jayatunga Ayers Bruens 104009 abstract AI-discovered 2024 pipeline analysis phase I 80-90% 24 molecules'; (4) 'BCG Jayatunga AI-discovered molecules clinical success analysis Wellcome methodology definition'; (5) 'AI-discovered molecules clinical Phase II success rate n= Jayatunga limitations small sample industry baseline comparison critique 2025'
failure_reason: The article is behind the Elsevier paywall. WebFetch of the ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403. No open-access full text, preprint, PMC deposit or author copy was located; every accessible source repeats the 80-90% figure without the denominator.
alt_sources_tried: (a) sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S135964462400134X - HTTP 403; (b) europepmc.org/article/MED/38723763 - navigation shell only, no record content; (c) ouci.dntb.gov.ua/en/works/96nDjjJ9/ - bibliographic metadata only (authors, DOI, journal), no abstract; (d) quantumbiospace.ai secondary summary - reports 80-90% and 40% with denominators explicitly absent; (e) pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12472608 (Niazi 2025 critical review) - does not cite the paper; (f) frontiersin.org 10.3389/fphar.2026.1870527 - cites the figures, not the n; (g) nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01496-2 (Bender et al. 2026) mirror - cites the paper as ref 10 without reproducing percentages or n
best_estimate: n between 21 and 30 molecules for the Phase I denominator
best_estimate_basis: The BCG/Wellcome tracking set contained ~73-75 AI-derived molecules in clinical pipelines as of 2023 [E-2004]. An independent count of 8 leading AI companies found 31 molecules in trials in April 2024 [E-2071]. Of ~75 tracked molecules, most were still in Phase I and had not reached a Phase I decision point; the subset with a resolved Phase I outcome is therefore a minority. A widely repeated secondary figure describes '24 AI-discovered targets' within the 67-drug clinical set [E-2004 context]. Taking the resolved-outcome subset at roughly one third of the tracked cohort gives n approximately 24. At n=24 and p=0.85 the Wilson 95% CI is 66.1-94.3% [E-2066], which is the number carried into the report. This estimate is explicitly an inference, not a retrieved value.

item: Jayatunga et al. 2024 Phase II denominator (n behind the ~40% figure)
queries_tried: Same five queries as the Phase I denominator item, plus 'AI-discovered drugs phase 2 failure rate similar Nature Medicine 2025 editorial analysis'
failure_reason: Paywalled; no accessible source states the Phase II n. All secondary sources that quote 40% omit the denominator, and one explicitly notes 'the sample size is small'.
alt_sources_tried: (a) ScienceDirect - 403; (b) ResearchGate publication 380223979 - request-full-text page only, no content; (c) humai.blog synthesis - gives 40% vs 37% with no n; (d) intuitionlabs 2026 census - independently counts 8 AI assets that have completed Phase 2 across the whole field [E-2055]; (e) noah.bio narrative review - repeats 40% without n
best_estimate_basis: Independent 2026 census counts 8 of 117 AI-enabled assets as having completed Phase 2 field-wide, five years after the Jayatunga data cut [E-2055]. The 2023 cut-off cohort must therefore have been smaller still. Niazi 2025 independently states only 4-9 AI-derived molecules have publicly documented clinical outcomes [E-2007]. Wilson 95% CI at p=0.40, n=8 is 15.2-71.3%; at n=10 it is 16.8-68.7% [E-2065]. Either interval spans every plausible industry baseline, which is sufficient to support the NO EVIDENCE verdict on axis (ii) regardless of the exact n.

item: Named list of companies included in the Jayatunga AI-discovered cohort, and the operational definition of 'AI-discovered'
queries_tried: (1) 'BCG Jayatunga AI-discovered molecules clinical success analysis Wellcome methodology definition'; (2) 'Jayatunga Ayers Bruens 104009 abstract AI-discovered 2024 pipeline analysis'; (3) 'number of AI-derived drug candidates entering clinical trials per year 2024 2025 census Deep Pharma Intelligence Nature Biotechnology count INDs'
failure_reason: Paywalled. Search snippets reveal only that the cohort included molecules partnered with pharmaceutical companies and excluded COVID-19-related molecules, and that target classes spanned kinases, epigenetic regulators, PPI modulators and GPCRs. The inclusion rule that separates 'AI-discovered' from 'AI-assisted' is not stated in any accessible source.
alt_sources_tried: (a) ScienceDirect - 403; (b) askme.it secondary - identifies the BCG/Wellcome partnership and ~73 molecules but no company list; (c) biopharmatrend - names 8 leading AI companies with 31 clinical molecules (April 2024) as an independent proxy [E-2071]; (d) intuitionlabs 2026 census - names 63 companies field-wide but for a 2025 data cut, not the 2023 cohort [E-2054]
best_estimate: Cohort most likely comprises Exscientia, Insilico Medicine, Recursion, BenevolentAI, Schrodinger, Relay Therapeutics, Verge Genomics, Evotec, Iktos/Lantern-tier companies and their pharma partners; definition most likely 'a molecule from a company that self-describes the programme as AI-enabled'
best_estimate_basis: The ~73-molecule tracked set [E-2004] is close to the ~75 cumulative AI-derived clinical molecules counted independently by end-2024 [E-2072], which implies a broad, self-report-based inclusion rule rather than a narrow 'AI generated the structure' rule. The ASCO/JCO 2026 landscape explicitly warns that such aggregated counts mix candidates where AI proposed both target and structure with programmes where AI merely accelerated an existing workflow [E-2054]. This definitional breadth is itself the central methodological weakness and is recorded as such in the report.

item: Published formal rebuttal or correspondence responding directly to Jayatunga et al. 2024 with a reanalysis
queries_tried: (1) 'critique AI-discovered drugs Phase I success rate survivorship bias selection bias Jayatunga rebuttal'; (2) 'AI-discovered molecules clinical Phase II success rate n= Jayatunga limitations small sample industry baseline comparison critique 2025'; (3) 'AI-discovered drugs phase 2 failure rate similar Nature Medicine 2025 editorial analysis'
failure_reason: No formal published rebuttal, correspondence, or reanalysis was located. Criticism exists but is distributed across review articles rather than concentrated in a single response paper.
alt_sources_tried: (a) Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 2026 (Bender/Thomas/Scannell) - cites the paper as reference 10 and states clinically relevant impact is disappointingly limited, but does not reanalyse it [E-2006]; (b) MDPI Pharmaceuticals 2026 validation-crisis review - argues no approvals and unchanged attrition, without a targeted reanalysis [E-2061]; (c) Niazi 2025 - independently counts only 4-9 documented outcomes, an implicit refutation of the statistical basis [E-2007]; (d) Thieme 'Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery and Development' - notes variable AI-designed definitions, likely survivorship and publication bias, and absence of controlled comparison
best_estimate: No formal rebuttal exists; the effective critique is distributed and rests on three points - undisclosed denominators, definitional breadth, and absence of a matched comparator cohort
best_estimate_basis: Three independent peer-reviewed reviews published after the original all decline to endorse the PoS conclusion while citing the paper [E-2006, E-2007, E-2061]. Combined with the derived power calculation showing the Phase II comparison is roughly 500-fold underpowered [E-2065], the absence of a formal rebuttal reflects the field treating the result as unfalsifiable at current n rather than as accepted.

item: Numeric success rate in 'RFdiffusion Exhibits Low Success Rate in De Novo Design of Functional Protein Binders for Biochemical Detection' (bioRxiv 2025.02.07.636769)
queries_tried: (1) 'RFdiffusion de novo binder experimental success rate percentage designs tested Baker lab 2023 2025'; (2) direct WebFetch of the .full.pdf URL (three attempts); (3) direct WebFetch of the v1 landing page
failure_reason: bioRxiv returned HTTP 429 Too Many Requests on every attempt across the session (Retry-After values of 77, 76, 42, 81, 23, 74, 90 seconds; retried after intervening work and still throttled). The abstract text was never served.
alt_sources_tried: (a) biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.07.636769.full.pdf - HTTP 429 x2; (b) biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.02.07.636769v1 - HTTP 429; (c) search-engine snippet - returns the title only, no numbers; (d) substituted the DigBioLab pooled meta-analysis of 3,766 designs across 15 targets, which supplies a superior and independently computed figure of 11.6% [E-2020]; (e) substituted the Adaptyv Bio independent contract-lab replication [E-2022]
best_estimate: Success rate below the 11.6% pooled average, plausibly in the 0-5% range for this application class
best_estimate_basis: The paper's title asserts a low rate, and the pooled meta-analysis shows per-target precision spanning 0.1 to 1.0, i.e. some targets yield essentially nothing [E-2020]. Functional (catalytic or detection-competent) binders are a strictly harder requirement than binding alone, and the Science prospective docking study shows the same functional-versus-binding gap in small molecules, where functional hit rates were 1-5% against binding hit rates of 26-54% [E-2013]. The report does not rely on this record for any conclusion; the 11.6% pooled figure carries the argument instead.

best_estimate: AlphaFold3 pose accuracy is expected to sit between AF2 models and experimental holo structures for virtual screening, i.e. materially better than AF2 on static pockets and materially worse than a liganded experimental structure on induced-fit pockets

The report's benchmark-versus-reality conclusion rests on the three fully retrieved AF2 benchmarks, not on this estimate.

best_estimate_basis: Derived in E-2057: numerator is the 117-candidate cumulative census [E-2054] annualised over 10 years (1.03%) and over 3 years (3.42%); denominator is 1,139 CY2024 CDER commercial IND receipts [E-2056].
